lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
How many right angles in a non-square rectangle? Can a triangle have two right angles? Explain.

FEEDBACK
4; no — two right angles would force the third to be zero/impossible in a simple triangle.

WATCH FOR
Counting exterior notches as interior angles double-counts corners.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
For twelve polygons, count vertices and classify each interior angle as acute/right/obtuse where clear. Justify four.

Write a short reflection naming one step you corrected and why.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
A rectangle has 4 right angles. An equilateral triangle has 3 equal acute angles. Spotting a right angle in a pentagon is possible even if not regular.

TRY FIRST
How many right angles in a non-square rectangle? Can a triangle have two right angles? Explain.

FEEDBACK
4; no — two right angles would force the third to be zero/impossible in a simple triangle.
teach_steps.explain:
Angles in shapes are the interior corners; counting and classifying them supports property language.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the places, values or distances that carry the method. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your working with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your reasoning? If a digit or place is uncertain, identify what would have to be regrouped or counted again. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Counting exterior notches as interior angles double-counts corners. Correct the value or method, not just the appearance of the digits.
